```{r}
library(tidyverse)
```

This page compares tourism patterns and travel infrastructure across four major ocean regions: the **Caribbean**, **Indian Ocean**, **North Atlantic**, and **Pacific Ocean**.

## 1. Caribbean: 2024 Stayover Arrivals by Destination

```{r}
# Load Caribbean dataset and keep the 2024 destination stayover breakdown
caribbean_data <- read_csv("data/carribean tourism data.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(
    record_type == "destination_arrivals",
    source_url == "https://www.hoperesearchgroup.com/blog/caribbean-tourism-statistics-2025",
    year == 2024
  ) |>
  # Convert raw visitor counts into millions and order bars from smallest to largest
  mutate(
    arrivals_millions = value / 1e6,
    destination = fct_reorder(destination, arrivals_millions)
  )

caribbean_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = arrivals_millions, y = destination, fill = change_percent)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_number(suffix = "M")) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "plasma", labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Caribbean Stayover Visitor Arrivals (2024)",
    subtitle = "Bar length shows total visitors; color shows annual growth rate (%)",
    x = "Stayover Visitors (Millions)",
    y = NULL,
    fill = "YoY Growth",
    caption = "Source: Caribbean Tourism Statistics (data/carribean tourism data.csv)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

This chart shows how many stayover visitors each Caribbean destination welcomed in 2024, with the longest bars representing the busiest markets. The color scale highlights each destination’s annual growth rate, so countries with warmer colors were growing faster while cooler ones were expanding more slowly or seeing little change.

## 2. Indian Ocean: 2025 Year-over-Year Shifts in Tourism Metrics

```{r}
# Keep headline 2025 India tourism metrics that report a year-over-year % change
indian_data <- read_csv("data/indian ocean tourism data.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(
    record_type == "observation",
    geography == "India",
    year == "2025",
    !is.na(change_vs_previous_year_pct),
    # Keep top-level GDP and jobs totals rather than redundant direct/indirect subtotals
    !indicator %in% c("Direct tourism GDP", "Indirect tourism GDP",
                      "Direct jobs in tourism", "Indirect jobs in tourism")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    direction = if_else(change_vs_previous_year_pct >= 0, "Increase", "Decrease"),
    indicator = fct_reorder(indicator, change_vs_previous_year_pct)
  )

indian_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = change_vs_previous_year_pct, y = indicator, color = direction)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  # Draw lollipop stems from 0% out to each metric's percentage change
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = change_vs_previous_year_pct, yend = indicator), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Decrease" = "#d95f02", "Increase" = "#1b9e77")) +
  labs(
    title = "Annual Percentage Change Across India Tourism Indicators (2025)",
    subtitle = "Domestic visits surged while foreign tourist arrivals and exchange earnings dipped",
    x = "Change vs. Previous Year (%)",
    y = NULL,
    color = "Direction",
    caption = "Source: India Tourism Data Portal (data/indian ocean tourism data.csv)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

This chart compares 2025 tourism indicators in India against the previous year, with positive values meaning growth and negative values meaning decline. It suggests that demand is still strong in domestic travel and related economic activity, while foreign arrivals and foreign exchange earnings were weaker than the prior year.

## 3. North Atlantic: Geographic Distribution of Travel Hubs

```{r}
# Classify OpenTravelData feature codes into readable hub categories
north_atlantic_data <- read_csv("data/north atlantic tourism data.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(
    record_type == "location_reference",
    !is.na(latitude), !is.na(longitude)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    hub_type = case_when(
      feature_code %in% c("AIRP", "AIRF", "AIRH", "AIRS") ~ "Airport / Airfield",
      feature_code == "RSTN" ~ "Rail Station",
      str_starts(feature_code, "PPL") ~ "City / Populated Place",
      TRUE ~ "Other Travel Point"
    )
  )

north_atlantic_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, color = hub_type)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, size = 0.9) +
  coord_quickmap() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(
    title = "North Atlantic Travel Infrastructure Map",
    subtitle = "5,301 travel points of reference colored by infrastructure type",
    x = "Longitude (°E / °W)",
    y = "Latitude (°N)",
    color = "Hub Type",
    caption = "Source: OpenTravelData (data/north atlantic tourism data.csv)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(alpha = 1, size = 3)))
```

This map shows where the main travel hubs in the North Atlantic are concentrated, with different colors marking airports, rail stations, and cities. The pattern highlights the dense transportation network that connects major destinations and helps explain why travel activity is concentrated around these corridors.

## 4. Pacific Ocean: Pandemic Shock & Recovery in Seat Arrivals (2019–2022)

```{r}
# Filter monthly international seat arrivals for six major Pacific Island destinations
pacific_data <- read_csv("data/pacific ocean tourism data.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(
    record_type == "observation",
    indicator == "Average 7-day international seat arrivals",
    geography %in% c("Fiji", "Papua New Guinea", "Samoa", "Vanuatu", "Palau", "Tonga")
  ) |>
  # Parse YYYY-MM strings into Dates so ggplot scales the time axis properly
  mutate(
    month_date = ym(period),
    seats_7day = as.numeric(value)
  )

pacific_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = month_date, y = seats_7day, color = geography)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9, show.legend = FALSE) +
  # Use free y-scales so smaller island markets are clearly visible alongside Fiji
  facet_wrap(~ geography, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  labs(
    title = "Pacific Island International Seat Arrivals (2019–2022)",
    subtitle = "Monthly average 7-day incoming seats showing 2020 border closures and 2022 reopening",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Avg. Seats per 7 Days",
    caption = "Source: World Bank Pacific Observatory (data/pacific ocean tourism data.csv)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

This figure shows how international seat arrivals collapsed during the pandemic and then recovered unevenly across Pacific island destinations. The sharp drop in 2020 reflects border closures, while the gradual rebound suggests reopening and renewed travel demand in the region.
